title: Lagarde looks for a broadening of the energy shock beneath 4% inflation
summary: Euro area inflation of 4% in October raised the stakes for the ECB, but the release offered no clear evidence yet that energy costs were feeding broadly into wages and underlying prices. Christine Lagarde said the outcome exceeded what the ECB had expected a few months earlier while matching market expectations. Those are different comparisons: an upside surprise to an older central-bank assessment need not be new information to investors on release day. Speaking on 4 November in an interview published on 7 November, she declined to pre-empt either the next forecast or the December decision.

The composition of inflation explains that caution. Energy inflation rose from 18.9% in September to 20.8% in October. Lagarde pointed to the Middle East conflict and reduced global refining capacity. Food inflation rose too. Core inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco held at 2.5%. Services inflation edged up to 3.3%, within its range of the preceding four months. The ECB still lacked the detailed breakdown needed to establish whether services prices were rising primarily in energy-intensive activities such as transport or whether costs were spreading more widely. A high headline rate sustained for several quarters would increase the risk to the medium-term target even in the absence of immediate broadening (inflation and second-round effects exchanges).

Forward-looking wage evidence had yet to show a shift beyond the second-round effects already incorporated in the ECB’s projections. Lagarde cited multi-year pay agreements and companies’ wage expectations. Her account of 2021–22 explains why that finding offered only conditional reassurance. Central banks initially expected supply-driven inflation to subside as the supply shock unwound. They underestimated the demand support from economies reopening while households spent accumulated savings. Her lesson was to reassess which shocks were operating together. In the current forecast, higher energy futures relative to September affected both inflation and growth, and long-term interest rates had also risen. The more recent dip in oil prices did not resolve the combined effect. She said a significant change in conditions would be needed to alter the direction she expected, while reserving decisions for individual meetings.

Asked about pressure on French government debt, Lagarde put the rise in long yields in a global context. Higher inflation, increased sovereign issuance and competition for funding from AI infrastructure borrowers were all possible contributors. Countries with larger debt stocks were more sensitive to higher global rates, strengthening her case for compliance with Europe’s fiscal rules. She offered no quantitative attribution for French yields. Asked about the Transmission Protection Instrument, she kept the ECB’s tools available subject to their criteria and a Governing Council judgement. The answer provided no country-specific intervention threshold.

Several longer-horizon issues concerned the institutions through which policy works. Lagarde discussed coordination against cyber risk and possible links between Europe’s instant payment settlement system and foreign payment systems. Cross-border digital central-bank payments were a future possibility. She described Council cohesion as an achievement and her early departure as a wish to speak more freely about public issues. In the exchange on representation, she counted two women among 27 people around the Council table and attributed the pattern partly to national appointment practices. She also raised ageing, productivity and immigration as shared European and Japanese challenges. These remarks supplied her institutional and personal perspective without changing the conditions she set out for the forthcoming policy decision.

questions.question: Which services were responsible for October’s increase?
questions.detail: The aggregate services rate stayed inside its recent range, but Lagarde lacked a detailed breakdown. A transport-led increase and a wider change in labour-intensive prices imply different persistence and different risks for short euro rates. Examine the detailed harmonised inflation release as it becomes available, comparing energy-intensive categories with the breadth of changes elsewhere against their earlier seasonal patterns.

questions.question: What evidence would justify revising the wage component of the forecast?
questions.detail: The ECB saw no shift beyond the second-round effects already embedded in its projections. The question is how large those embedded effects were and which new settlements would overturn that judgement. Consult the September projection assumptions, the wage agreements covering the relevant horizon and contemporary company surveys. Distinguish changes in the basic wage from one-off compensation before assessing the case for tighter policy.

questions.question: How much of the rise in French long yields was common to other issuers?
questions.detail: Lagarde describes worldwide financing competition and greater sensitivity among heavily indebted states. She leaves open how much French borrowing costs reflected global rates versus a change in the premium on French debt. For sovereign relative-value exposure, compare matched-maturity yields and swap rates, issuance calendars and auction results. Examine the ECB’s published conditions for its transmission instrument separately from any inference about willingness to intervene.
